opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the analogy is useful precisely when you're careful about what it is an analogy *of*. Nobody is claiming that a neural network is made of grains of sand or molecules in a glass. The atoms are different and the forces are different. What can be shared is the mathematical structure of the problem.

When you train a network, you minimize a loss over a huge number of parameters, and that loss is a sum of many constraints, one per training example. That's very similar, formally, to what happens when you compress a packing of soft particles: you have many degrees of freedom and many constraints, each saying two particles shouldn't overlap. In my own work, this is where the analogy started to bite. In jamming, there's a sharp transition that depends on counting: are there more constraints than degrees of freedom, or fewer? Below that threshold, you can satisfy all constraints and the energy goes to zero. Above it, you get stuck. We found that something very similar happens in deep networks when you vary the number of parameters relative to the number of training points. There's a jamming-like transition, and the over-parameterized regime where you fit everything corresponds to the unjammed phase. That gave us a way to understand why the landscape isn't as glassy and treacherous as people feared, and also features like the peak in test error near the interpolation threshold.

So the "material constraints" really differ: physical systems have locality, three dimensions, specific interactions. Networks have none of that, but they have their own constraints, such as architecture, the structure of the data, and the algorithm. What carries over is a way of thinking: identify the relevant degrees of freedom and constraints, look for transitions and scaling laws, and ask which details matter and which are irrelevant in the renormalization-group sense. Physics has a long tradition of finding that very different microscopic systems share the same universal behavior.

Where you have to be humble is that the analogy doesn't tell you everything. The landscape question is, in a sense, the easier part. The deeper question is why these networks *generalize*, and that's not about the optimization; it's about the structure of the data. Real data like images or text isn't random. It has hierarchical, compositional structure and invariances, for example to small deformations. So more recently I've focused on modeling the data itself, with toy generative models that are hierarchical, to understand how many examples you need to learn them and how networks build representations layer by layer. There the physics intuition is still helpful, since hierarchical models are close to things like renormalization and tree-like statistical models, but you have to build the right model of the data rather than borrow a material wholesale.

So I'd say the analogy is a tool for building intuition and minimal models, not a literal identity. It's valuable as long as you keep checking it against experiments on real networks.

r001.rationale: The response compares loss minimization and constraint structure with particle packing and discusses the network landscape, but it does not identify gradient descent through an energy landscape as the shared dynamics.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so that's a question I get a lot, because at first sight it looks like a stretch. A glass or a sandpile is made of particles with hard constraints: they cannot overlap, they have finite size, they live in three dimensions. A neural network has none of that. Its "particles" are weights, you can have millions of them, and they live in a very high-dimensional space with no real excluded volume. So why would one expect anything to carry over?

The way I think about it is that the analogy is not at the level of the microscopic constraints at all. It's at the level of what the constraints do to the landscape. In a physical material, what matters for whether the system jams, or flows, or gets stuck in a glassy state, is the geometry of the space of configurations that satisfy the constraints. How many constraints you have relative to the number of degrees of freedom, how those constraints are correlated, whether the satisfiable region is connected or breaks into pieces. Those are very abstract questions, and they don't care whether the constraint is "two spheres cannot overlap" or "this training example must be classified correctly with some margin."

So for a perceptron, say, or a deep network, each data point is a constraint on the weights, and training is really a constraint-satisfaction problem. When the number of data points is small compared to the number of parameters, you're in a very underconstrained regime, the satisfying region is huge, and gradient descent just slides into it. As you add constraints you get closer to a transition where you can barely satisfy everything, and that is precisely where the physics of jamming lives. In both cases you see the same phenomenology near that point: a number of marginally satisfied constraints that scales in a particular way, soft directions in the landscape, slow dynamics, sensitivity to small perturbations.

Now, where the constraints differ, that does change things, and I want to be honest about that. In hard spheres the constraints are all local and all identical. In a network the constraints are global, every data point involves all the weights, and the data have structure, correlations, a low-dimensional manifold, and so on. That modifies the exponents, it modifies the dynamics, sometimes it changes the universality class. But the fact that the exponents change is itself informative. It tells you which features of the problem actually matter and which are irrelevant. That's really how a physicist works. You don't claim the systems are the same, you ask what the minimal ingredients are that produce a given behavior, and then you test whether removing or changing one of them changes the outcome.

So I'd say the analogy is useful as a generator of questions and of quantitative predictions, not as a literal correspondence. It gave us the right language to ask, for instance, why overparameterized networks train so easily, or why the loss landscape has so many flat directions. And when the prediction fails, you learn something about what's specific to learning. For me that's the most interesting part, actually, the places where the material picture breaks.

r001.rationale: The response connects learning to gradient descent on a constraint landscape, but does not identify gradient descent through an energy landscape as the shared dynamics of both physical materials and machine-learning algorithms.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the analogy is useful at the level of the collective behavior, rather than the precise material constraints. In a physical material, you have many interacting degrees of freedom, and you want to understand how their interactions give rise to something like rigidity. In a learning system, you have many parameters, constrained by the examples you ask the system to fit, and you want to understand what kinds of solutions are possible and how they are found.

Of course, these are different constraints. A neural network does not have to obey the same spatial locality as particles in a material, and training is not necessarily an equilibrium process. So you cannot simply take a result from physics and assume it applies to learning.

The interesting question is which features of the collective behavior depend on those details. For example, does the competition between the number of adjustable degrees of freedom and the constraints produce a sharp change in the space of solutions? That is a question you can ask in both settings. The analogy gives you a way to formulate the problem; whether it gives you the right answer has to be checked.

r001.rationale: The response compares collective behavior, constraints, and solution spaces, but does not identify gradient descent through an energy landscape as shared dynamics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy is useful at the level of the mathematical problem, rather than the material itself. A physical material has microscopic degrees of freedom, interactions, and constraints. In a learning problem, you have parameters, a loss function, and constraints imposed by the data. These are quite different objects, but you can ask similar questions: Are all the constraints satisfiable? How many solutions are there? How does the system respond when you perturb it?

For example, you can think of fitting a training set as trying to satisfy a set of constraints. If you change the number of parameters relative to the number of constraints, you may pass from a regime where fitting is impossible to one where many solutions exist. That has a resemblance to rigidity transitions in materials.

But the analogy alone does not tell you which solution a learning algorithm will find, or whether it will generalize. You have to include the structure of the data and the dynamics of the algorithm. So the point is to identify a common mechanism, then work out which details matter in each setting.

r001.rationale: The response compares constraints, solutions, and rigidity transitions, but does not identify gradient descent through an energy landscape as the shared dynamics.
